newsitem.title: JAPAN: US group urges flexibility in US-Japan air talks.
newsitem.headline: US group urges flexibility in US-Japan air talks.

text.p: A U.S. business group said on Tuesday the time for decision making had come in bilateral air talks between the United States and Japan, and urged both sides to be more flexible.

"The time for philosophical debate has past. The time for decisions is at hand," said Gerald Baliles, chairman of the Aviation Coalition for Competition and Expanded Services Between the United States and Japan (ACCESS U.S.-Japan), an industry body calling for expanded air services between the two nations.

Baliles, a former Virginia governor, said an expanded air market would result in benefits worth billions of dollars to both countries and that while both sides were talking, they were still engaged in a philosophical debate that prevented further progress.

He said the United States had accepted more aviation rights for All Nippon Airways and Nippon Cargo Airlines in line with other carriers covered by the current 1952 bilateral treaty but wants Japan to agree that the ultimate goal would be open skies.
Open skies, a U.S.-backed policy, calls for the lifting of all regulations for airlines except for safety rules.
Tokyo wants the upgrading in rights for the two carriers and is prepared to offer expanded opportunities for other U.S. airlines not covered by the 1952 treaty but not at the cost of open skies.
Japan rejects open skies, arguing that such pacts lead only to monopolistic alliances which stifle competition and are dominated by U.S. mega-carriers.

Trans World Airlines, Delta Airlines, American Airlines and Continental Airlines are all members of ACCESS-U.S.-Japan, along with other groups and some governments, but not UAL Corp's United Airlines and Northwest Airlines, the incumbent carriers which have greater privileges under the treaty.
Baliles added, however, that United had joined American Airlines in a coalition arguing for expanded air ties between the U.S. Midwest and Asia.
